records.title: A Practical Framework of Key Performance Indicators for Multi-Robot Lunar and Planetary Field Tests
records.summary: Robotic prospecting for critical resources on the Moon, such as ilmenite, rare earth elements, and water ice, requires robust exploration methods given the diverse terrain and harsh environmental conditions. Although numerous analog field trials address these goals, comparing their results remains challenging because of differences in robot platforms and experimental setups. These missions typically assess performance using selected, scenario-specific engineering metrics that fail to establish a clear link between field performance and science-driven objectives. In this paper, we address this gap by deriving a structured framework of KPI from three realistic multi-robot lunar scenarios reflecting scientific objectives and operational constraints. Our framework emphasizes scenario-dependent priorities in efficiency, robustness, and precision, and is explicitly designed for practical applicability in field deployments. We validated the framework in a multi-robot field test and found it practical and easy to apply for efficiency- and robustness-related KPI, whereas precision-oriented KPI require reliable ground-truth data that is not always feasible to obtain in outdoor analog environments. Overall, we propose this framework as a common evaluation standard enabling consistent, goal-oriented comparison of multi-robot field trials and supporting systematic development of robotic systems for future planetary exploration.

records.title: Assembling Solar Panels by Dual Robot Arms Towards Full Autonomous Lunar Base Construction
records.summary: Since the successful Apollo program, humanity is once again aiming to return to the Moon for scientific discovery, resource mining, and inhabitation. Upcoming decades focus on building a lunar outpost, with robotic systems playing a crucial role to safely and efficiently establish essential infrastructure such as solar power generating towers. Similar to the construction of the International Space Station (ISS), shipping necessary components via modules and assembling them in situ should be a practical scenario. In this context, this paper focuses on the integration of vision, control, and hardware systems within an autonomous sequence for a dual-arm robot system. We explore a perception and control pipeline specifically designed for assembling solar panel modules, one of the benchmark tasks. Ad hoc hardware was designed and tested in real-world experiments. A mock-up of modular solar panels and active-passive connectors are employed, with the control of this grappling fixture integrated into the proposed pipeline. The successful implementation of our method demonstrates that the two robot manipulators can effectively connect arbitrarily placed panels, highlighting the seamless integration of vision, control, and hardware systems in complex space applications.

records.title: AutoNGC: One Small High-Fidelity Testbed, One Giant Leap for Autonomous GN&C at the Moon
records.summary: NASA’s pursuit of sustained human presence on the Moon and Mars necessitates robust, autonomous navigation capabilities to meet operational challenges beginning in the cislunar environment. These challenges include decreasing dependency on human-in-the-loop ground control, onboard rapid GN&C (guidance, navigation and control), and able to select from a wide range of measurement types. NASA Goddard’s autoNGC (autonomous navigation, guidance, and control) system represents a foundational step in this direction. To overcome these challenges, we have developed a high-fidelity autoNGC testbed for any complex GN&C situation, which has been tailored for the unique demands of lunar missions. This testbed enables comprehensive verification and validation of measurements, novel algorithms, and flight-like hardware. NASA continues to sponsor commercial missions and experimental on orbit technology development to accelerate the maturation of lunar position, navigation, and timing (PNT) technologies. The autoNGC testbed offers a flexible platform for testing the software and hardware integration required for next-generation missions. The testbed has successfully supported the demonstration of delivery of new autonomous capabilities to existing hardware during flight operations for CAPSTONE (Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System Technology Operations and Navigation Experiment). Likewise, the testbed is paving the way for GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) based navigation solutions and forward predictions for lunar missions such as Intuitive Machines’ LCRNS (Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems). The testbed facilitates rigorous evaluation of navigation sensor scenarios and performance profiling to identify optimization opportunities. It utilizes NASA GSFC’s suite of simulation tools and integrates processing platforms ranging from development boards to flight-ready electronic boxes. This flexible architecture makes the autoNGC testbed available for testing other GN&C systems with a variety of emulation techniques. This work details the system architecture of the autoNGC testbed and its software ecosystem of cFE/cFS applications. Next, it highlights the various hardware processing platforms and their capabilities for emulating or accepting a diverse array of navigation measurement types such as GNSS, optical, RF tracking, and time/frequency. Simulation results for representative lunar mission scenarios are presented, with discussion of the specific testbed configuration, lessons learned, and directions for future enhancement to enable rapid technology readiness advancement.
keywords: autoNGC Autonomy Testbed Navigation Guidance Control GN&C

records.title: Autonomous Fault and Anomaly Detection in Extraterrestrial Drilling
records.summary: Subsurface sampling can detect biomarkers protected from harsh surface conditions and is a crucial step in the search for extraterrestrial life on planetary bodies. NASA’s proposed “Icebreaker” mission aims to explore Mars’ subsurface through robotic drilling. In extraterrestrial planetary environments, computing, energy, and environmental constraints require robotic agents to complete tasks unsupervised. Currently, there is no broadly applicable solution for detecting faults early enough to prevent hardware failure in drills specialized for planetary sampling, such as Honeybee Robotics’ The Regolith and Ice Drill for Exploring New Terrain (TRIDENT) chosen for NASA’s 2027 VIPER mission. TRIDENT has been validated at various Mars and lunar analog field sites, including Devon Island in the Canadian High Arctic, the Atacama Desert, and the Schirmacher Oasis and Lake Untersee in the Antarctic in January 2026.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Autonomy for Lunar Surface Infrastructure Construction
records.summary: An autonomous system architecture for robotic construction of lunar surface infrastructure is presented. Infrastructure is key to creating a permanent human presence on the moon. Permanent structures such as launch and landing facilities, environmental shelters, and tall towers to support solar panels or communications equipment will support astronaut activities. An economical way to establish infrastructure is through autonomous robotic construction. A team of robots with various capabilities would transport materials from a lander to a prepared construction site, manipulate structural components for alignment, and actuate tools for joining the structure. After establishing basic truss structures, the robot team would then outfit the structures with cable harnesses for power and data transfer, flexible hoses for fluid transfer, panels (i.e, solar panels, radiators, walls), regolith coverings for radiation mitigation, and other functional modules.

records.title: Capability-Aware Planning and Control of Multi-Robot Teams for Resilient Lunar Cargo Transport
records.summary: The NASA Space Technology Mission Directorate has identified Autonomous Robotics for Surface Logistics and Sustainability as a key research area for enabling human exploration of the Moon and Mars. Human habitation for long durations necessitates autonomous robotic teams to handle the complex logistics of cargo transport, tracking, storage, and maintenance. But, the scale of these missions eclipse all other surface operations performed to date, requiring new advancements in autonomy to reduce robotic dependence on human oversight. This proposal details how capability-aware control and planning for multi-robot teams can be matured from low-TRL to meet these needs, which directly addresses the Civil Space Shortfall (1538) Robotic Mobile Manipulation for Autonomous Large-Scale Logistics, Payload Handling, and Surface Transport. Robots must plan and execute all aspects of cargo transport, including coordinating transport of oversize items, interacting with landers, handing equipment to humans, packing, deploying instruments, and managing a heterogeneous fleet. Relying on robots in this way requires them to deal with degradation caused by the lunar environment. Capability-aware control of individual robots, coupled with capability-aware task planing for the overarching team permits recognition of and adaptation to degradation. While aspects of these technologies have been touched on in the literature, capability-aware planning and control for multi-robot teams remains at a conceptual stage of maturity, or Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 2. Once developed, these components still must be combined into a cohesive system that meets the communication and processing constraints of space-worthy hardware. This work is divided into four aims. Aim 1 develops capability-aware control of individual robots by incorporating capability metrics as parameters and limits for tube-based model predictive control. Aim 2 uses change point detection on state residuals to quickly identify when capabilities change. Aim 3 then re-estimates the changed capabilities; an initial estimation is obtained by minimizing the detected residual change with respect to each capability, and refined with set-membership estimation. Aim 4 brings capability-awareness to the team level by incorporating capabilities into task selection and validating that the resulting plan will achieve the goal with ...
keywords: Activity and Resource Planning and Scheduling

records.title: cFS, ROS2 Integration as Space Robotics Standardization Candidates
records.summary: From Artemis launching manned missions to the Lunar and Martian surfaces, SpaceX sending private astronauts into Earth’s orbit, and to China returning lunar samples; the dawn of a new space age is upon us. Not dominated by just a few superpowers but by international accords coupled with private industry, and fueled by humanity’s innate curiosity. The vastness of space cannot be tamed through human resources alone. Autonomous systems powered by robust, fault-tolerant algorithms and AI are the only ways we can fully capitalize on the space domain. The use of autonomous systems is necessary for establishing a foothold in space, and those footholds will enable large off-world outposts to support further research missions, expansion, and environmental exploitation. Crew and robotic autonomy and cooperation at Martian outposts will become paramount due to considerable communication delays and disruptions. With one-way transmission taking up to 22 minutes to arrive while in transit to Mars, and between 15 to 20 minutes on the surface of the planet.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Design and Development of Modular Limbs for Reconfigurable Robots on the Moon
records.summary: In this paper, we present the development of 4-DOF robot limbs, which we call Moonbots, designed to connect in various configurations with each other and wheel modules, enabling adaptation to different environments and tasks. These modular components are intended primarily for robotic systems in space exploration and construction on the Moon in our Moonshot project. Such modular robots add flexibility and versatility for space missions where resources are constrained. Each module is driven by a common actuator characterized by a high torque-to-speed ratio, supporting both precise control and dynamic motion when required. This unified actuator design simplifies development and maintenance across the different module types. The paper describes the hardware implementation, the mechanical design of the modules, and the overall software architecture used to control and coordinate them. Additionally, we evaluate the control performance of the actuator under various load conditions to characterize its suitability for modular robot applications. To demonstrate the adaptability of the system, we introduce nine functional configurations assembled from the same set of modules: 4DOF-limb, 8DOF-limb, vehicle, dragon, minimal, quadruped, cargo, cargo-minimal, and bike. These configurations reflect different locomotion strategies and task-specific behaviors, offering a practical foundation for further research in reconfigurable robotic systems.

records.title: DewTwin-Coin: an onboard autonomous framework for lunar water-ice prospecting using Chandrayaan-3 LIBS and ChaSTE data
records.summary: It is important to locate water-ice in the lunar regolith to build futuristic, sustainable bases there. But communication delays from Earth, limited bandwidth, and power constraints demand an onboard, autonomous, time-efficient decision-making framework for locating volatiles such as water-ice in the lunar regolith. In this work, we present a framework, DewTwin-Coin, that can locate potential water-ice sites in real time without drilling. Its decision-making principle is based on a find-S learning algorithm that uses surface temperature and the Hydrogen-to-Oxygen intensity ratio at a location. The core idea is a physics-based rule $-$ water-ice is stable only if the temperature is below 110 K and the Hydrogen-to-Oxygen intensity ratio is between 1.7 and 2.3. We validate DewTwin-Coin on Chandrayaan-3's 3165 laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) elemental data with 387 Chandra's surface thermophysical experiment (ChaSTE) data. On a 16 GB RAM system, it classified all 3165 locations within 615 seconds, yielding no strong signatures of water-ice, which matches the Chandrayaan-3 in-situ analysis. This framework is very important for future lunar and other planetary missions in which an onboard rover can autonomously determine feasible drilling locations for water-ice without issuing false drilling commands in warm terrains. Thus, the mission's onboard setup can stretch its technical limits in both power and memory capacity.

records.title: Distributed Multi Robot Lunar Cargo Transportation via Phase Decomposed Reinforcement Learning
records.summary: Modular reconfigurable robotic systems provide a scalable solution for cooperative surface operations in future lunar missions. However, cooperative cargo transportation remains challenging due to morphology-dependent topology changes, strong payload-induced coupling, long-horizon decision making, and safety constraints. This paper proposes a phase-decomposed reinforcement learning framework for cooperative cargo transport with distributed robotic units. The task is decomposed into lifting, transportation, and placement, each optimized with a dedicated joint-state policy capturing inter-agent coupling. Centralized training promotes stable convergence, while deployment uses onboard proprioception for control and OptiTrack motion capture for ground-truth evaluation and post-processed metrics. A deterministic phase controller expressed in Markov state representation regulates transitions between stages, and a failure-sensitive synchronization mechanism ensures coordinated progression and safety-aware halting during real-world execution. The framework is evaluated in simulation and through controlled field experiments at a JAXA space exploration test facility. Results demonstrate reliable cooperative transport across all stages in both simulation and hardware experiments.

records.title: Dynamic Multi-Objective Prioritization for Autonomous Robot Teams on the Moon and Mars
records.summary: As NASA transitions to sustained exploration on the Moon and Mars, autonomous robot teams facilitating surface operations must continuously balance competing priorities under persistent uncertainty. Because environmental conditions, resource availability, and mission objectives change over time, committing to a predetermined balance of objectives becomes inadequate. This research investigates adaptive multi-objective prioritization for autonomous robot teams performing surface logistics tasks, such as caretaking and payload handling, enabling resilient, sustainable autonomy on the Moon and Mars in dynamic mission settings. This capability is critical because robust autonomy depends on adapting which objectives matter when, not just how to achieve a fixed set of objectives. The principal aim of this proposal is to enable robot teams to autonomously redistribute objective priorities in response to changing conditions and/or changing mission needs. The specific objectives of this work are to: (1) generate a robust set of tradeoff-efficient strategies for multi-objective robot team control; (2) map tradeoff-efficient strategies to the conditions to which they are best suited; and (3) design a generalized runtime decision module that autonomously selects strategies in response to team state and evolving mission constraints. The first objective extends ongoing work investigating the use of entropy-based metrics to generate a robust set of neural network controllers (i.e., policies) for a team of robots operating across multiple objectives. The second objective aims to infer the implicit decision-making strategies embedded within each policy and to map these policies to the mission contexts where each controller succeeds. The final objective delivers a runtime decision module for a team of robots by dynamically switching policies based on the mapping learned from the second objective. In summary, this research will enable robot teams to autonomously redistribute objective priorities in response to changing conditions in order to optimize overall team outcomes. The key contribution of this work is to transform multi-objective decision-making from a static, design-time choice into a dynamic runtime capability, allowing robot teams to reason about tradeoffs in the field with minimal human intervention. By enabling fully autonomous operation, this capability directly ...
keywords: Activity and Resource Planning and Scheduling

records.title: Emergent Cooperative Thermoregulation in Lunar Swarm Robotics
records.summary: Swarms of small robots are an attractive way to survey lunar caves and lava tubes. Missions such as NASA's CADRE will fly cooperating rovers for distributed mapping, but only in daylight. The 354 h lunar night drops the surface towards 95 K, and the radioisotope heaters that let single rovers survive it cannot be supplied at swarm scale. In this study we investigate whether a swarm can instead use its own members as thermal shielding. We train one policy, shared by all twenty robots, by reinforcement learning with an evolution-strategies estimator. The policy receives a single reward, once, at the end of the night: the mean temperature of the five coldest robots. Nothing in that reward refers to position, spacing, exposure or motion. Two behaviors nonetheless emerge. The swarm aggregates, and robots circulate between the sheltered core and the exposed rim, the same pair of behaviors with which emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter. We measure the survival threshold, the smallest stored energy per robot at which every robot is still alive at sunrise. Across ten runs it is 155.6 +/- 1.3 pcm-h, where one pcm-h is 7.2 kJ of stored heat. That is 37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound, and at a budget where the motionless huddle loses six robots, every robot survives. The behavior needs no shared spatial reference and no robot-robot contact, and transfers from twenty robots to forty without retraining.

records.title: Emerging trends in Cislunar Space for Lunar Science Exploration and Space Robotics aiding Human Spaceflight Safety
records.summary: In recent years, the Moon has emerged as an unparalleled extraterrestrial testbed for advancing cuttingedge technological and scientific research critical to enabling sustained human presence on its surface and supporting future interplanetary exploration. This study identifies and investigates two pivotal research domains with substantial transformative potential for accelerating humanity interplanetary aspirations. First is Lunar Science Exploration with Artificial Intelligence and Space Robotics which focusses on AI and Space Robotics redefining the frontiers of space exploration. Second being Space Robotics aid in manned spaceflight to the Moon serving as critical assets for pre-deployment infrastructure development, In-Situ Resource Utilization, surface operations support, and astronaut safety assurance. By integrating autonomy, machine learning, and realtime sensor fusion, space robotics not only augment human capabilities but also serve as force multipliers in achieving sustainable lunar exploration, paving the way for future crewed missions to Mars and beyond.

records.title: Enabling Reliable, Fault-Tolerant Autonomous Lunar Habitats with High-Performance Spaceflight Computing
records.summary: The lunar surface presents unfavorable constraints and harsh living conditions. To address these challenges, autonomous habitats will require complex integrated systems that combine advanced software, high-performance hardware, and cutting-edge sensors to ensure sustainability, safety, and operational efficiency. Consequently, maintaining a sustainable presence on the Moon requires reliable infrastructure and efficient development, precise monitoring, and utilization of resources within a lunar installation. These elements are essential not only to ensure that lunar settlement can be long-term, self-sustaining, and resource-efficient, but also to serve as a foundation for future missions and eventual human habitation on Mars. Humans are not native to the Moon; therefore, our survival and ability to thrive will depend on autonomous systems that can foster safety and resilience through high-availability architectures, graceful degradation, and highly fault-tolerant spaceflight hardware capable of continuing operation during failures. This requires advanced human-rated distributed systems architectures with specialized electronics, scalable capabilities, and an integrated design approach. Unlike current practices focused on short-term missions and regularly maintained components, permanent lunar compute systems must be designed for extended operations beyond mission durations. This paper explores the necessity of transitioning toward fault- tolerant, highly autonomous hardware systems designed for multi-year missions. It also identifies critical subsystems that require high levels of autonomy, supported by radiation-hardened processors and extreme thermal loads, which are essential to mitigate long-term degradation and ensure sustainable lunar habitation. Finally, the paper aligns with NASA’s identified Civil Space Shortfalls, particularly in high-performance onboard computing, advanced data acquisition, extreme-environment avionics, radiation monitoring and countermeasures, and autonomous health management. It proposes NASA’s new High-Performance Spaceflight Computing (HPSC) processor as a turnkey solution, delivering 100 times the performance-per-watt of legacy rad-hard CPUs and enabling onboard AI, edge computing, and fault-tolerant features essential for sustained lunar autonomy and beyond.

records.title: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Quadrupedal Jumping in Lunar Gravity
records.summary: Legged robots can extend planetary exploration to rugged and discontinuous terrain that is inaccessible to conventional rovers. In lunar gravity, jumping further expands this mobility by enabling robots to cross obstacles and gaps that cannot be traversed by walking alone. We present a multistage reinforcement-learning approach that produces a single end-to-end control policy for commanded point-to-point jumping under lunar gravity. The resulting policy has a simple architecture and relies exclusively on mission-compatible onboard sensing, making its deployment on a real lunar mission plausible. In simulation, the learned policy performs accurate point-to-point jumps with landing errors smaller than the robot's body size. We analyze the torque and power demands of lunar jumping and characterize performance degradation under extreme outlier events, including control-update freezes of up to \SI{1}{s} during flight. Hardware transfer demonstrates that the policy can successfully execute a vertical jump under lunar-gravity offloading. Furthermore, the measured torque and power profiles are consistent with the simulation results and remain within the robot's hardware limits.

records.title: Gaze-Assisted Supervisory Control for Lunar Robotic Arm Teleoperation Under Concurrent Monitoring
records.summary: Rover-mounted robotic arms can extend human reach during lunar sample handling, but continuous joystick teleoperation requires repeated visual-motor alignment while operators may also need to monitor system states. This paper presents a gaze-assisted supervisory control framework in which gaze nominates a rock or placement target, explicit confirmation authorizes the action, and the robot performs bounded autonomous grasp-and-place execution. The framework was evaluated against manual joystick teleoperation in a mission-analog virtual reality study with 16 participants. The study used a 2 x 2 x 3 within-subject design varying control mode, placement difficulty, and concurrent monitoring load. Mean recorded task completion time decreased from 47.65 to 18.43 s per rock, with 72.5% of this difference arising during grasping. Under the tested auditory monitoring conditions, gaze-assisted supervisory control showed less average proportional slowing, with no detected control-mode difference in monitoring-response accuracy or speed. The rate of gaze shifts between core areas of interest decreased from 49.98 to 27.73 shifts/min, while the raw NASA Task Load Index score decreased from 32.54 to 18.26. However, the benefit was task dependent. In precision placement, manual control yielded lower mean placement error and a higher placement success rate. These findings support a mixed-initiative allocation in which gaze enables rapid task-level intention specification and autonomous execution, while precision-critical stages retain manual refinement.

records.title: Hardware-Accelerated Instance Segmentation for Resource-Constrained Space Robotics with Criticality Analysis
records.summary: Autonomous lunar missions require real-time per- ception under three coupled constraints: extreme low-light conditions, limited onboard compute, and radiation-induced hardware faults that can silently corrupt inference. We present a deployment-oriented instance segmentation framework for resource-constrained lunar robotics that jointly addresses quan- tization calibration and system-level fault exposure under strict compute constraints. First, we introduce Activation Variance Informative Sampling (AVIS), a label-free calibration strategy that deterministically selects calibration samples based on activation variance statistics. Second, we deploy a YOLO-based segmentation model on a Deep Learning Processor Unit (DPU) with architectural modifications that reduce CPU fallback paths and enable statically compiled execution with bounded latency in low-lighting conditions. We further introduce a software-level criticality analysis to estimate fault exposure and guide mitigation under radiation-constrained operation. On a lunar micro-rover platform, AVIS with bias correction recovers 69.8% of quantization-induced accuracy loss while achieving 309 ms inference latency and 5.7 W power consumption. Targeted mitigation reduces global criticality by 31.7%. The results demonstrate an integrated approach and a blueprint for a reliable and safe AI perception framework under space deployment constraints.

records.title: He3-Seeker: Robotic Information Planning for Lunar Helium-3 Distribution Mapping
records.summary: Lunar helium-3 is a highly valuable strategic resource, pivotal to the advancement of both deep-space exploration and space mining. Existing lunar helium-3 exploration methodologies rely primarily on indirect measurements via remote sensing, which are often characterized by limited precision, low reliability, and insufficient spatial resolution. In this paper, we introduce He3-Seeker, an active robotic exploration method for helium-3 distribution mapping. First, we provide a formal definition of the active helium-3 exploration problem. Subsequently, we developed the He3-Seeker framework, which is conceptually based on multi-point drilling, sampling, and in situ analysis. In particular, we use robotic information planning (RIP) to guide autonomous robot navigation and active sensing. Additionally, to thoroughly evaluate the proposed algorithm, we introduce a reliable method for generating reference data of lunar helium-3 distribution based on low-resolution orbital remote sensing measurements. Simulation experiments verify that He3-Seeker achieves both rapid and high-fidelity mapping of helium-3 distribution, providing a reliable solution for resource exploration tasks. Our code and simulation environment will be publicly accessible at https://github.com/OpenSpace-Lab/He3-Seeker.

records.title: Heterogeneous Autonomy for Robotic Multi-agent Operations through learNed adaptivitY
records.summary: Heterogeneous Autonomy for Robotic Multi-agent Operations through learNed adaptivitY (HARMONY) develops new autonomy for heterogeneous teams of surface robots that can carry out lunar and Martian logistics with minimal Earth tactical planning. The central objective is to enable mixed-capability teams, such as a fast scout rover, a cargo carrier, and a support rover, to coordinate reliably even when their mobility, sensing, and onboard compute resources differ. This work is intended to start at TRL 2 and mature through integrated demonstrations. The technical approach combines three complementary methods: (1) a learning-enabled predictive driving control layer (meta-learned model predictive control) that adapts in real time to changing terrain dynamics (e.g., slip and sinkage) on resource-constrained, flight-relevant compute; (2) a hierarchical planning layer that decides when scouts should gather information, when heavier assets should commit to a safe route corridor, and how the team should update plans as conditions change; and (3) coordination and task assignment so the most suitable robot executes each task in an asymmetric team. Evaluation will include hardware-in-the-loop testing on flight-relevant compute and integrated physical experiments using open-source rover testbeds. This work directly supports NASA's Autonomous Robotics for Surface Logistics and Sustainability objectives and the shortfalls focused on robotic large-scale logistics transport and surface-based lunar logistics management (1546, 1608, 1609).
keywords: Activity and Resource Planning and Scheduling

records.title: Intelligent Multi-Agent Constellations for Cooperative Cislunar Operations
records.summary: Future missions to cislunar space and beyond will rely on satellite constellations to support navigation, communication, and operations. To reduce costs and operational burdens while increasing mission versatility, these constellations must be capable of autonomous, cooperative, and strategic decision-making under the highly nonlinear dynamics of the Earth-Moon system. However, existing constellation design methods typically rely on low-fidelity dynamical modeling or neglect the autonomous decision-making structures required for reconfigurable multi-agent operations. This research proposes a framework for intelligent cislunar satellite constellations that integrates dynamical systems theory with cooperative multi-agent control methods. By leveraging quasi-periodic orbits (QPOs) arising in cislunar models and recent parameterization methods that transform these nonlinear dynamics and trajectories into a linear representation on an invariant torus, cooperative dynamic games can be used to autonomously coordinate and reconfigure constellations to efficiently complete shared objectives. The project is structured into three phases. In the first phase, parameterized QPO dynamics will be leveraged to design constellations and ensure bounded relative motion. In the second phase, dynamic game-theoretic methods will be integrated to find control policies that enable autonomous formation reconfiguration and cooperative objective completion. In the third phase, these control policies and dynamical structures will be transitioned across a hierarchy of cislunar models with the goal of validating under high-fidelity ephemeris models. The resulting framework aims to enable mission-adaptive autonomy for future cislunar satellite constellations, directly supporting NASA's objectives for sustained lunar exploration and operations.
records.org: The University of Texas at Austin

records.title: Interface Agnostic Robotic Grasping: Rigid-Soft Grippers for Logistics and Power Connection Tasks on the Lunar Surface
records.summary: Sustained lunar surface operations will require robotic systems capable of handling a wide variety of logistics objects, including electrical power connectors, cargo carriers, fluid tanks, and maintenance spares. Current lunar architecture concepts increasingly rely on robotic manipulation to ensure infrastructure can be assembled, reconfigured, and maintained independent of crew presence. While standardized rigid grasping interfaces can support reliable manipulation, they also introduce mass penalties, restrict design freedom, and create integration overhead for every new item added to the logistics manifest. These constraints motivate an architectural shift toward end effectors that can accommodate diverse object geometries without requiring specialized mechanical features. This study evaluates a split finger fin ray effect gripper as a flexible, interface agnostic manipulation option positioned to reduce system level burdens within emerging lunar surface architectures. The gripper employs compliant materials and an internal deformable structure that allows passive shape adaptation during grasping. This structured compliance reduces dependence on object-specific geometry and can mitigate small alignment sensitivity when objects are imperfectly localized or dusty. However, these benefits introduce uncertainties in grasp stability, slip behavior, and repeatability, particularly for mission critical operations such as connector mating. To address these concerns, this work characterizes the gripper’s mechanical behavior under load testing and contact-rich manipulation. These findings support the inclusion of compliant end effectors as a viable architectural component for future lunar operations. Their ability to manipulate varied objects without dedicated interfaces offers a pathway to reduced mass impacts, simplified hardware design cycles, and increased operational flexibility for robots under supervised autonomy. A development path is proposed that prioritizes maturation of environment tolerant materials, refinement of gripper geometry, and expanded testing within representative lunar logistics workflows.

records.title: Lunar Assembly and Service by Autonomous Robotics (LASAR)
records.summary: In-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (ISAM) missions require robotic systems that can perform precise joining and repair tasks despite communication latency, thermal variation, diverse lighting conditions, uncertain workpiece geometry, and limited crew intervention. This work presents the Lunar Assembly and Servicing by Autonomous Robotics (LASAR) system, a ground demonstration of autonomous robotic laser beam welding and additive manufacturing capabilities relevant to future ISAM missions. LASAR integrates PickNik MoveIt Pro with the Rocket Lab Robotics xLink robotic arm. Both technologies are also used by NASA’s Fly Foundational Robots mission, establishing a direct connection between terrestrial ISAM testing and future orbital robotic operations. The autonomy architecture combines model-based motion planning, collision-aware trajectory execution, autonomous seam detection, visual servoing for weld-tool alignment, coordinated laser and robot control, and supervisory remote operations. Operators at NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) remotely commanded experiments performed at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC). Thermal-vacuum tests evaluated robotic welding at extreme temperatures from approximately −40 ◦C to 55 ◦C, while additional tests incorporated a wire-feed mechanism for additive deposition and weld repair. The demonstrations advance perception-guided manipulation, remote operations, and in-space welding capabilities needed for scalable ISAM infrastructure.

records.title: LUNARMBENCH - Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation for Lunar Surface Logistics & Infrastructure
records.summary: NASA’s Moon Base operations will require robotic systems to manipulate logistics items, payloads, cables, connectors, and infrastructure interfaces before crew arrival, during uncrewed periods, and alongside astronauts. At the same time, robotic manipulation is advancing rapidly through physical AI, learning-based control, improved simulation, and robot foundation models, but existing benchmarks remain largely terrestrial and do not evaluate the lunar-relevant tasks, interfaces, environmental stressors, or operational constraints NASA must understand. This CIF will establish LunArmBench, an Ames-led V0 benchmark and evaluation framework for lunar surface robotic manipulation. The project will translate Moon Base Autonomous Systems & Robotics capability targets into simulation-based benchmark tasks, focused on cable/connector mate-demate, cable handling/routing, logistics payload handling, and payload/interface alignment. The benchmark will define task protocols, manipulation primitives, scoring metrics, lunar-relevant stressors, and baseline evaluation methods. Using NVIDIA Isaac Sim/Isaac Lab and a low-cost bimanual manipulation platform, the team will produce initial simulation assets, benchmark specifications, baseline results, and a hardware validation roadmap. LunArmBench will provide Ames and NASA with reusable evaluation infrastructure to guide physical AI development, inform robot-compatible interface design, and support follow-on Moon Base robotics maturation. Benefits: The goal of LunArmBench is to establish an Ames-led V0 benchmark and evaluation framework for lunar surface robotic manipulation. LunArmBench will translate Moon Base manipulation needs into representative task definitions, manipulation primitives, simulation assets, scoring metrics, and baseline evaluations. The initial focus will be on three task families: cable/connector mate-demate and cable routing; logistics payload handling and staging; and payload/interface placement and alignment. Our hypothesis is that a compact, mission-grounded benchmark can provide actionable evidence about which ...

records.title: Modular Isoperimetric Soft Robotic Truss for Lunar Applications
records.summary: We introduce a large-scale robotic system designed as a lightweight, modular, and reconfigurable structure for lunar applications. The system consists of truss-like robotic triangles formed by continuous inflated fabric tubes routed through two robotic roller units and a connecting unit. A newly developed spherical joint enables up to three triangles to connect at a vertex, allowing construction of truss assemblies beyond a single octahedron. When deflated, the triangles compact to approximately the volume of the roller units, achieving a stowed-to-deployed volume ratio of 1:18.3. Upon inflation, the roller units pinch the tubes, locally reducing bending stiffness to form effective joints. Electric motors then translate the roller units along the tube, shifting the pinch point by lengthening one edge while shortening another at the same rate, thereby preserving a constant perimeter (isoperimetric). This shape-changing process requires no additional compressed air, enabling untethered operation after initial inflation. We demonstrate the system as a 12-degree-of-freedom solar array capable of tilting up to 60 degrees and sweeping 360 degrees, and as a 14-degree-of-freedom locomotion device using a step-and-slide gait. This modular, shape-adaptive system addresses key challenges for sustainable lunar operations and future space missions.

records.title: Pneumatic Rigid-Soft Coupled Finger with Self-Powered Triboelectric Tactile Sensing toward Potential Application in Lunar Exploration
records.summary: Robotic manipulation in future lunar-surface operations and planetary sample-return missions requires end effectors capable of accommodating irregular objects while maintaining reliable tactile feedback under uncertain contact conditions. Motivated by these challenges, we present a terrestrial proof-of-concept of a pneumatic rigid-soft coupled robotic finger integrating structural regulation and self-powered triboelectric tactile sensing. The finger combines rigid skeletons, fiber-constrained pneumatic chambers, and a finger-pad sensing unit to enable compliant deformation, posture regulation, and tactile perception. A flexible single-electrode triboelectric sensor based on a PDMS-MXene composite generates electrical signals through contact electrification and electrostatic induction without external electrical excitation, while pneumatic actuation, signal acquisition, and computational processing require external power. At an input pressure of 140 kPa, the proximal interphalangeal, distal interphalangeal, and metacarpophalangeal regions achieved bending angles of approximately 84°, 76°, and 65°, respectively. The sensor exhibited stable outputs at contact frequencies of 1-10 Hz and a sensitivity of 0.11 V/kPa over 10-120 kPa. Incorporating 6 wt% MXene increased the output voltage by 50.8% compared with pure PDMS. Combined with a convolutional neural network-long short-term memory model, the system achieved classification accuracies of 97.6% for 10 representative laboratory materials and 99.5% for four surface-roughness levels under controlled terrestrial conditions. Grasping experiments further demonstrated compliant manipulation and tactile perception. These results establish the feasibility of the proposed sensing approach under laboratory conditions, while its applicability to planetary geological materials and space environments remains to be validated.

records.title: Robotic leaping enhanced by thrust-induced hypogravity, achieving precise, predictable, and extended jumps
records.summary: Robotic jumping research advances engineering and biomimicry frontiers, prioritizing range, precision, and predictability to navigate unstructured environments. Earth's gravity necessitates powerful actuators and lightweight bodies in robotic designs for maximal jump height. While many robots excel in statical environments, precise, predictable jumps in dynamic settings remain challenging. We realized this with a bipedal robot leveraging thrust-induced hypogravity, alongside dual regulation of aerial attitude and parabolic trajectory via thrust vectoring. Hypogravity multiplies leap range (max: 6.9 m) despite leg force saturation, enabling the robot to clear multi-level stairs, a 2.35-m-high wall, and 3-m-wide stream. Parabolic trajectory regulation allows leap distance precision/consistency surpassing existing thrust-assisted hybrids and leg-only jumpers. It enables pre-jump prediction of aerial/landing positions and timing, facilitating leaps in dynamic scenarios: through fast-moving windows (3.8 m/s), onto shifting, confined targets, and against wind disturbance. This research establishes extended range, precise, and predictable jumping through self-generated hypogravity and parabolic trajectory regulation.

records.title: SpaceVLA: Generalized Intelligent Autonomy for Space-Based Asset Decision-Making
records.summary: My proposed work is to develop an integrated foundation-model and simulation infrastructure for autonomous operations in space-based environments, initially focused on lunar surface and Moon-base applications aligned with Artemis. The effort is two-fold, pairing (1) a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, which serves as the decision-making "brain" for assets such as rovers, landers, satellites, and robotic manipulators, with (2) a physics-grounded world model that provides a high-fidelity, interactive simulation environment for space-specific conditions. Unlike world models designed primarily around terrestrial environments, the space world model will represent mission-relevant factors such as lunar terrain and regolith, reduced gravity, illumination, thermal conditions, dust, sensor behavior and noise, communications, power, vehicle state, operational constraints, uncertainty, and faults. The VLA will be developed as a general pretrained model that downstream customers and stakeholders can fine-tune and post-train for their specific hardware, procedures, and objectives, then deploy within the world model to generate scenarios and synthetic training data, conduct reinforcement learning, and test and validate autonomous behaviors before flight. This workflow has produced state-of-the-art results and step-function gains in autonomy and efficiency across both autonomous driving and humanoid robotics, and preliminary research indicates it can be applied to space-based environments to greatly enhance autonomous operations. In addition to the models themselves, the work will establish reusable infrastructure, interfaces, and workflows that let NASA missions and both internal and external stakeholders adapt, evaluate, and deploy these capabilities for their own assets, creating a scalable autonomy foundation that can extend from lunar operations to Mars, orbital systems, and other deep-space environments. This effort is being pursued in collaboration with NVIDIA. Benefits: VLA model for autonomous decision-making in rovers, satellites, and landers; real-time autonomous mission operations without continuous Earth-based control; reinforcement learning-based refinement across diverse mission scenarios; establishes GSFC as the frontier center for space-based autonomy via ASTRA.

records.title: SPICE-HL3: Single-Photon, Inertial, and Stereo Camera dataset for Exploration of High-Latitude Lunar Landscapes
records.summary: Exploring high-latitude lunar regions presents a challenging visual environment for robots. The low sunlight elevation angle and minimal light scattering result in a visual field dominated by a strong contrast featuring long, dynamic shadows. Reproducing these conditions on Earth requires sophisticated simulators and specialized facilities. We introduce a unique dataset recorded at the LunaLab from the SnT - University of Luxembourg, an indoor test facility designed to replicate the optical characteristics of multiple lunar latitudes. Our dataset includes images, inertial measurements, and wheel odometry data from robots navigating different trajectories under multiple illumination scenarios, simulating high-latitude lunar conditions from dawn to nighttime with and without the aid of headlights, resulting in 88 distinct sequences containing a total of 1.3 M images. Data was captured using a stereo RGB-inertial sensor, a monocular monochrome camera, and, for the first time, a novel single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) camera. We recorded both static and dynamic image sequences, with robots navigating at slow (5 cm/s) and fast (50 cm/s) speeds. All data is calibrated, synchronized, and timestamped, providing a valuable resource for validating perception tasks from vision-based autonomous navigation to scientific imaging for future lunar missions targeting high-latitude regions or those intended for robots operating across perceptually degraded environments.

records.title: SPLICER - Surface Power for Lunar Infrastructure Capability Enhancement with Robotic
records.summary: Moon Base will require power cables to be routed from power generation facilities (solar and / or nuclear) to power consumers. Consumers and generators may be widely distributed, including a landing / launch site, which is planned to be multiple kilometers from the base. Ideally, to preserve astronaut time for more challenging tasks, cable routing should be done by robots before astronauts arrive. We propose SPLICER: Surface Power for Lunar Infrastructure Capability Enhancement with Robotics, which will build on Ames’ surface rover heritage to develop autonomous cable deployment capabilities. We will iterate on an existing prototype design to unwind a spool and deploy a cable in a controlled manner. We will develop techniques for cable trenching, cable mating, and spool replacement. Utilizing a robotic arm and onboard vision, 1) a trench will be dug into regolith, to protect the cable and prevent a safety hazard for astronauts, 2) multiple spools of cable will be combined modularly where the cable of one spool connects to another spool harness, enabling the replacement of a single section of cable if damaged, and 3) spool replacement will detach / attach a spool to the rover and enable rover reusability for the Moon Base initiative. Benefits: The objective is to demonstrate 3 key capabilities needed for robust, effective, and reusable power cable deployment using Lunar surface rovers. Cable trenching – Digging a deep enough trench to install the cable for the best safety, longevity, and thermal properties. Cable mating – Combining multiple cables to easily extend power over distances longer than a single spool. Cable spool replacement – Replacing the cable spool with robotic arms, demonstrating that a rover can conduct multiple installations over its lifetime.

records.title: Towards Autonomous Extraterrestrial Drilling Through Imitation Learning
records.summary: One of NASA's long-term goals for planetary exploration is fully autonomous subsurface sample acquisition and analysis, which requires drilling systems capable of operating with minimal human intervention in uncertain subsurface environments. This work addresses this challenge for The Regolith and Ice Drill for Exploring New Terrain (TRIDENT), a 1-meter rotary percussive drill developed by Honeybee Robotics for NASA's VIPER mission. Autonomous extraterrestrial drilling must operate with little prior knowledge of the subsurface and limited visibility into borehole conditions. Additionally, fault data are costly to obtain, as they often require operating hardware to failure, limiting the applicability of data- intensive learning approaches. Previous research and field validation of subspace- based fault and anomaly detection methods have established a foundation for subsurface perception through drilling telemetry, enabling the exploration of autonomous drilling strategies. For robotic decision making and autonomy, we selected Imitation Learning (IL), which trains an agent to reproduce actions demonstrated by an expert. IL was chosen because the TRIDENT drill lacks a high- fidelity simulation environment, operates along a single axis with a limited action space, and has access to only a small quantity of labelled fault data. To support autonomous drilling operations, we developed a ROS2 middleware framework and integrated existing subsurface fault and anomaly detection methods. For autonomous decision making, we evaluated several imitation learning approaches and found methods utilizing modified forms of Behavior Cloning and Preference Comparison to perform best through offline validation testing. Work presented will include results from best performing methods on the TRIDENT drill in various composites and lunar simulant materials.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Training Data Selection for Weakly-Supervised Lunar Traversability Estimation: A Cross-Domain Study
records.summary: Abstract This paper examines how weakly supervised traversability estimation models generalize across domains in the context of lunar robotics. Because annotated lunar datasets are scarce, models must be trained on Earth-based data and transferred to environments with significantly different visual and physical characteristics. We adopt a pairwise, weakly supervised learning framework in which relative traversability annotations provide a lightweight alternative to dense labeling while preserving the continuous nature of terrain assessment. We conduct a systematic cross-domain evaluation over seven datasets spanning synthetic simulations, terrestrial analogs, lunar analog facilities, and real lunar mission imagery (Chang'e 3/4), using the Human Disagreement Rate (HDR) metric. Our results reveal a consistent ranking of training sources: lunar analog facilities transfer most reliably to real lunar imagery, while visual and morphological similarity to the target domain proves a stronger predictor of transfer quality than dataset realism or domain category. Notably, strong in-domain performance does not predict cross-domain generalization, exposing a fundamental limitation of standard evaluation protocols for space-graded perception systems. We further show that this ranking is stable across HDR thresholds, and that introducing limited target-domain data monotonically improves transfer performance while preserving the initial source ranking. Overall, this study provides an empirical basis for training data selection in lunar traversability applications and argues for cross-domain evaluation as a standard component of the verification and validation pipeline for planetary surface perception systems.

records.title: A low-power, high-dynamic range sensor system for long-term autonomy, navigation, and mapping on the lunar surface
records.summary: This work proposes a stereo event camera rig for robust mapping and navigation on the lunar surface. Initial testing in Phase I validated our system’s ability to generate accurate depth maps from event data alone. New calibration techniques specific to event cameras were developed, adapting traditional computer vision approaches to handle asynchronous event data streams. In sum, this configuration shows great promise for use on autonomous and teleoperated systems operating on the lunar surface, where harsh lighting conditions are common and information is sparse. Phase II development will introduce a self-calibration regime for all sensors on the rig, allowing the system to produce accurate data over longer periods of time. Tangram Vision will also test the abilities of the proposed sensor system extensively on autonomous platforms in harsh terrestrial conditions as a proxy for the lunar surface. Tangram Vision intends to use the funding largely to develop and refine these novel self-calibration routines, depth synthesis algorithms, and odometry algorithms for the purpose of long-term autonomy. By the end of Phase II, our sensor system will have been tested on an autonomous platform in a lunar-like environment (the deserts of California). The majority of the grant will be devoted to algorithmic development, alongside integration testing with deployed platforms. Target markets for this innovation include any terrestrial or extraterrestrial system that is expected to behave autonomously for long durations and/or in changing environments. This includes space exploration systems (lunar rovers, autonomous landing systems, and other forms of space robotics), defense and military robotics (autonomous ground vehicles, systems operating at night, and high-speed platforms), and commercial autonomous systems (industrial robotics, mining, construction, humanoids, last-mile delivery, mobility, etc.). Benefits: NASA’s Artemis missions will return humans to the moon in order to establish long-term presence. Long-term autonomy is key to this mission, as NASA surface assets and vehicles will continue operations before, during, and after human presence on the lunar surface. In order to achieve this, new and novel sensing technologies are needed to enable long-term autonomy of LTVs and other robotic systems even through the extreme lighting conditions encountered at the lunar south pole. The proposed sensor suite uses commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) sensors in a new and innovative way, one that Tangram ...

records.title: An integrated process for design and control of lunar robotics using AI and simulation
records.summary: We envision an integrated process for developing lunar construction equipment, where physical design and control are explored in parallel. In this paper, we describe a technical framework that supports this process. It relies on OpenPLX, a readable/writable declarative language that links CAD-models and autonomous systems to high-fidelity, real-time 3D simulations of contacting multibody dynamics, machine regolith interaction forces, and non-ideal sensors. To demonstrate its capabilities, we present two case studies, including an autonomous lunar rover that combines a vision-language model for navigation with a reinforcement learning-based control policy for locomotion.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence Analysis of Lunabotics University Competition Robot Performance
records.summary: Space Mining for resources such as water ice, and regolith, which contain many elements in the form of metals, minerals, volatiles and other compounds, is a necessary step for In-Situ Space Resource Utilization (ISRU). One of the primary goals is to extract propellants from the regolith and water ice, such as oxygen and hydrogen which could then be used for in-space transportation. In addition, the space mining system can be used for various construction tasks that can benefit human and robotic exploration as well as scientific investigations based on excavated exposed topography, such as the side walls of trenches. Berms are structures that are made from bulk regolith without any additional material brought from Earth and they could have many uses in lunar infrastructure applications such as shielding from rocket plume regolith ejecta, blast containment, creating shadowed regions for thermal stability, and shielding from Solar Particle events at high lunar latitudes. The National Aeronautics & Space Administration (NASA) Lunabotics Competition is a university-level competition designed to engage and retain students in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). NASA has directly benefited from this competition by encouraging the development of innovative lunar excavation concepts from universities which has resulted in clever ideas and solutions which could be applied to an actual lunar excavation device or payload. The challenge is for students to design and build a remote controlled or autonomous excavator, called a lunabot, that can collect, and deposit Black Point 1 (BP-1) lunar regolith simulant in a target area to build a berm structure. Larger volumes of regolith deposited in this area by each team will receive more construction points, which contribute to the overall prize score. The complexities of the challenge include the abrasive characteristics of the lunar simulant, the weight and size limitations of the lunabot, and the ability to control the lunabot from a remote control center or achieve full autonomy which is highly rewarded in the points scoring system.

records.title: Aurora Robotics X-Hab Technical Final Report
records.summary: The Aurora Robotics Lab at the University of Alaska Fairbanks participated in the 2024–2025 NASA X-Hab Academic Innovation Challenge to explore modular robotic construction for lunar surface infrastructure. Our project focused on designing and partially demonstrating a teleoperable and automatable robotic system capable of assembling a micrometeoroid-resistant arch structure from modular steel truss segments. Our Excahauler robot, developed for the NASA Break the Ice Lunar Challenge, was equipped with a modular manipulator and end-effector designed for aligning and connecting trapezoidal trusses. Given time constraints, we used a 3D-printed scale model to validate structural behavior and backfill performance using regolith simulant. Time and resource constraints prevented completion of a full-scale robotic assembly, but our team demonstrated essential capabilities including robotic lifting, modular interface design, and structural load testing. The project also resulted in lessons in systems engineering, scope management, and interdisciplinary collaboration, contributing both technical insight and educational value to future lunar construction efforts.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Autonomous Legged Mobile Manipulation for Lunar Surface Operations via Constrained Reinforcement Learning
records.summary: Robotics plays a pivotal role in planetary science and exploration, where autonomous and reliable systems are crucial due to the risks and challenges inherent to space environments. The establishment of permanent lunar bases demands robotic platforms capable of navigating and manipulating in the harsh lunar terrain. While wheeled rovers have been the mainstay for planetary exploration, their limitations in unstructured and steep terrains motivate the adoption of legged robots, which offer superior mobility and adaptability. This paper introduces a constrained reinforcement learning framework designed for autonomous quadrupedal mobile manipulators operating in lunar environments. The proposed framework integrates whole-body locomotion and manipulation capabilities while explicitly addressing critical safety constraints, including collision avoidance, dynamic stability, and power efficiency, in order to ensure robust performance under lunar-specific conditions, such as reduced gravity and irregular terrain. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in achieving precise 6D task-space end-effector pose tracking, achieving an average positional accuracy of 4 cm and orientation accuracy of 8.1 degrees. The system consistently respects both soft and hard constraints, exhibiting adaptive behaviors optimized for lunar gravity conditions. This work effectively bridges adaptive learning with essential mission-critical safety requirements, paving the way for advanced autonomous robotic explorers for future lunar missions.

records.title: Autonomous Systems Study
records.summary: This task involves conducting a multi-center study in FY25 to assess the performance and feasibility of autonomous systems in relation to Artemis architecture needs and M2M objectives. The study will elucidate the Strategy and Architecture Office (SAO) Lunar Architecture Team (LAT) evaluations for STMD Autonomous Systems & Robotics (AS&R). The team will integrate prior STMD-funded efforts and existing commercial/academic partners to establish a broad base of expertise for formulating future development efforts. Key outcomes will include identifying technologies requiring further development and formulating forward efforts to advance autonomous systems capabilities and other architecture-driven autonomous systems use cases leading to transition to industry for NASA and commercial mission applications. Benefits: ​​​​​​​This task will assess current autonomous system capabilities and identify new technology needs in relation to Moon to Mars (M2M) objectives and specific architecture-identified use cases and functions. The characterization of these existing gaps in performance and architecture risks associated with autonomous systems and the quantification of the impact of autonomous systems to address capability needs provides information to identify areas for further technology maturation and formulates forward-work recommendations to facilitate technology infusion. The work in this task also aligns ...

records.title: Boom-Enabled Actuating Manipulator
records.summary: The Boom Enabled Actuating Manipulator (BEAM) system delivers a novel extended-reach deployable robotic manipulation system, answering NASA’s call for innovative solution to overcome challenges of exploring increasingly scientifically challenging and important terrains. In Phase II, the BEAM subsystems will be demonstrated at TRL 5 via operation in a simulated planetary environment. The critical subsystems will then be integrated for a system operational demonstration, validating the BEAM design at the system level. Dynovas has aligned strategic partnerships within the Phase II effort to enable delivery of BEAM system designed for a specific mission integration target – such as CLPS, rovers, or VSAT – that supported by mechanism designs with flight heritage. The BEAM system utilizes a deployment boom capable of extending up to 10m in length with integrated smart material actuators to enable articulation along the length of the boom, achieving up to 10° of deflection at the tip of the boom. The bistable deployable boom is supported at the root by the deployer housing structure, in which it coils up for compact packaging when stowed. The boom deployer is mounted on a rotating gimbal platform, enabling ±90° of rotation in elevation and azimuth for both vertical and horizontal deployment. The gimbal mechanism in combination with the articulation along the length of the deployable structure unlocks extra degrees of freedom, providing a modular and adaptable arm capable of reaching locations previously inaccessible without astronaut intervention. The BEAM systems are configurable to deliver a robotic manipulation system solution for not only sample collection and handling, but also inspection via cameras or probes. The BEAM system is scalable for each application, enabling its integration and commercialization on platforms from micro-rovers to MER-class rovers, CLPS, or LTV for Lunar and Mars exploration and future deep space missions for other celestial bodies. Benefits: Enhanced Mobility and Manipulation in Space: With its advanced deployable structures and compatibility with various end-effectors, the BEAM system can facilitate intricate sample collection, scientific experiments, and repair tasks on celestial bodies or in orbit, aligning with NASA's goals for Mars exploration, lunar surface missions under the Artemis program, and robotic missions to asteroids and moons. Efficiency and Cost-effectiveness: The BEAM system's SWaP-C optimization contributes to reducing mission costs and improving spacecraft efficiency. This is crucial for extending the duration ...

records.title: BUILDER: Leveraging BIM information to automate robot task planning for lunar assembly applications
records.summary: In order to support permanent human presence on the Moon, a number of critical infrastructures must be built on the lunar surface. Robots are expected to play a crucial role in the construction process, performing autonomous assembly and outfitting of a variety of systems, such as tall towers for solar power generation, shelters for crew and asset protection, and lander plume containment shields for launch & landing pads. As it has been noted in state-of-the-art work, the knowledge of building data is critical for the application of robotic solutions in terrestrial construction and operation. Specifically, these works leverage the information contained in Building Information Modeling (BIM) files that describe a target infrastructure, to extract and provide the robotic agent with the geometric, semantic and scheduling data that can then be used to assist in the generation of assembly plans to be carried out by the robot. In this proposal, TRACLabs proposes BUILDER (Leveraging BIM information to automate robot task planning for lunar assembly applications), a set of software tools that facilitate the integration of BIM data - describing an assembly infrastructure - with ROS, the standard software framework to build robot applications. The BUILDER tools are expected to provide 3 types of utilities: (1) Translate geometric data (3D models and poses) from the BIM files into objects natively usable by ROS-based tools, such as motion planning libraries; (2) Translate scheduling and semantic BIM data - describing the assembly and its construction - into a format suitable to be used for generic task planning tools; (3) Build upon our existing task planning tools, we'll integrate the geometric, scheduling and semantic data now accessible to ROS-based tools, into our framework, enabling it to autonomously generate task plans that are specific to a robotic platform, with the robot plans being encoded using a hierarchical approach based on Behavior Trees. Benefits: The tools proposed in this project, which leverage building information to facilitates the generation of robot task plans to assemble infrastructure on the lunar surface, are expected to have many applications to NASA missions including: 1. Autonomous robotic assembly of crucial infrastructure on the lunar surface during Artemis missions, such as power grids and shelter for crew and equipment. 2. Autonomous robotic assembly of habitat environments for future Mars missions. 3. Future missions involving robotic agents in the Gateway, in which the robots leverage the building data corresponding ...

records.title: Compact robots with long reach for space exploration and maintenance tasks
records.summary: This project focuses on the integrated design, control and motion planning needed for a new class of robots intended for maintenance and inspection tasks on the Moon and Mars and for structures in orbit. The robots have a low mass and compact stowed form factor but a long reach and the ability to apply forces and torques at widely separated locations. They are suitable for operation in challenging terrain such as caves or lava tubes, with the ability to anchor themselves using sparse handholds and then perform tasks like drilling for placing anchors or attaching and detaching components. Although they have a large workspace, these robots also impose constraints not found in conventional manipulators. For example, they may be able to pull much harder or apply torques much larger in some directions than in others, depending on their stance. The proposed research includes dynamic modeling and simulation to develop motion plans and inform the design of these robots---for example, how to configure joints to maximize the dexterous workspace for a chosen set of tasks. Dynamic simulation also provides a basis for generating motion plans, using a combination of optimization and machine learning methods. Core milestones will include (1) mechanical development of a high-performance manipulator utilizing a predominantly prismatic structure enabled by booms designed for many deployment cycles, (2) adaptive control methods for precise position and force control, (3) motion planning studies of such multi-limbed mobile platforms for dexterous manipulation, and (4) initial field deployment of accumulated advancements on physical robot system. Close collaboration with NASA is integral to this project, particularly through the NSTGRO Visiting Technologist Experience, which will provide direct mentorship and access to NASA's advanced technical resources. Engaging with NASA technologists will ensure the robot's capabilities are aligned with NASA's mission needs, allowing us to refine our tasks toward specific lunar and planetary applications of interest. Through a combination of innovative robotic design, advanced motion planning, and NASA collaboration, this project seeks to push the boundaries of robotic autonomy in extreme environments. The outcome will be a class of robots capable of versatile, forceful, and adaptive interactions that can support maintenance and exploration ...

records.title: Cosmic-XT, A Truss-Traversing General-Purpose Outfitting Robot
records.summary: Cosmic Robotics, Inc. proposes the development of Cosmic-XT, an autonomous, self-powered robot designed for truss traversal and outfitting in lunar and space environments. The primary function of Cosmic-XT is to climb, navigate, and outfit Tall Lunar Towers (TLTs) with electrical wiring, sensors, lighting, and other secondary systems. Equipped with truss-grippers, an extendable arm, and a harness installer, the robot moves using an inchworm-like motion to attach and secure electrical components to truss structures. Additionally, the Particle AI error detection system enables real-time identification of issues such as tangled wires and foreign object debris. The NASA SBIR Phase I funding will be utilized to advance the technology to TRL 4 maturity, with milestones including a conceptual system design review, a proof-of-concept harness installer mechanism, and a conceptual design review of the AI-based error detection system. This funding supports proof-of-concept development, de-risking technical challenges such as autonomous wire handling, efficient power usage, and AI-driven error detection. The target market includes NASA and commercial space infrastructure providers, focusing on lunar base construction, on-orbit servicing, and autonomous maintenance. Beyond space, potential applications extend to commercial construction, power line maintenance, oil and gas, and disaster response, where robotic outfitting can enhance safety and efficiency in hazardous or hard-to-reach environments. The lunar market alone is estimated at $170 billion, making Cosmic-XT a viable solution for the long-term sustainable development of space infrastructure. Benefits: Cosmic-XT directly aligns with NASA’s mission directives by advancing autonomous robotic capabilities for lunar infrastructure assembly, outfitting, and maintenance. The Artemis program aims to establish a sustainable lunar presence, requiring scalable, autonomous solutions for constructing and maintaining surface structures. Cosmic-XT addresses this need by climbing, outfitting, and inspecting Tall Lunar Towers (TLTs), which are critical for power generation, communications, and habitat support. Its truss-traversing design and modular payload system enable it to perform key tasks such as ...

records.title: Efficient Learning-Based Control of a Legged Robot in Lunar Gravity
records.summary: Legged robots are promising candidates for exploring challenging areas on low-gravity bodies such as the Moon, Mars, or asteroids, thanks to their advanced mobility on unstructured terrain. However, as planetary robots' power and thermal budgets are highly restricted, these robots need energy-efficient control approaches that easily transfer to multiple gravity environments. In this work, we introduce a reinforcement learning-based control approach for legged robots with gravity-scaled power-optimized reward functions. We use our approach to develop and validate a locomotion controller and a base pose controller in gravity environments from lunar gravity (1.62 m/s2) to a hypothetical super-Earth (19.62 m/s2). Our approach successfully scales across these gravity levels for locomotion and base pose control with the gravity-scaled reward functions. The power-optimized locomotion controller reached a power consumption for locomotion of 23.4 W in Earth gravity on a 15.65 kg robot at 0.4 m/s, a 23 % improvement over the baseline policy. Additionally, we designed a constant-force spring offload system that allowed us to conduct real-world experiments on legged locomotion in lunar gravity. In lunar gravity, the power-optimized control policy reached 12.2 W, 36 % less than a baseline controller which is not optimized for power efficiency. Our method provides a scalable approach to developing power-efficient locomotion controllers for legged robots across multiple gravity levels.

records.title: Hardware Systems and EDU Demonstration of the Tall Lunar Tower Project
records.summary: The Tall Lunar Tower (TLT) project developed a robotic tower assembly system (RTAS) and TLT Truss engineering development units (EDUs) to perform a ground demonstration of supervised semi-autonomous robotic assembly of a truss-based tall tower. Truss structures provide exceptional strength-to-weight ratios for payload capabilities supporting large masses. On the lunar surface, tall towers are a critical structural system that will enable significant solar power generation by supporting vertical solar arrays and beyond-the-horizon communications at the lunar south pole, supporting the Artemis mission architecture, as well as a lunar economy. Tall towers, greater than 30-meters-tall, provide the elevation needed for more consistent solar power generation due to low inclination sunlight and deep shadowing from surface features on the lunar surface at the poles. The robotic structural assembly technologies developed for truss-based tall towers will also enable other large-scale functional lunar structures to be built, including launch plume deflectors, lunar safe havens for astronauts and assets, surface transportation for cargo, and other critical infrastructure. Robotic assembly of truss structures for lunar surface infrastructure is near-term enabling for future Artemis mission campaign and Moon to Mars Objectives needs for power and communication. The project team designed, fabricated, tested, and demonstrated the RTAS EDU by assembling a TLT Truss EDU in a laboratory environment.
